transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-21
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~38 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Shaw (Redwood SE), Lena Morales (Ironworks Head of InfoSec), Tom Barlow (Cloud Eng), Priya Singh (Compliance)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect):
- Walkthrough of what admin and operational telemetry Redwood captures (who/what/when, IP, session id, api key fingerprints).
- Export options discussed: near-real-time streaming (syslog/Kinesis), S3 batch export, JSONL snapshots for SIEM ingestion.
- Retention and legal hold options: configurable retention, export for long-term archival, support for truncated/redacted prompt data per policy.
- KMS integration, key rotation, and HSM options mentioned; SSO/RBAC group-sync for admin audit mapping.
- Next steps: send example exports, run pilot ingest, confirm retention/residency requirements, share SOC2 copy.

Topics: audit-log contents; export formats; retention/archival; KMS and key management; RBAC & SSO mapping; legal/forensic requests

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Patel: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros then we'll jump in. we're hoping to cover what Redwood captures for admin operations, how you can get that data out, and retention controls.
[00:17] Lena Morales: thanks Maya. we are trying to map your telemetry to our SIEM and also need to understand data residency for long term storage. we have a three year retention ask from legal but need to see format and volume.
[00:34] Ethan Shaw: yep; high level we capture actor identity (user id / service account / api key fingerprint), action type (api call, model deploy, rollback, role change), timestamp, request metadata (ip, user agent), and when relevant a delta of configuration. we also record model version and route used.
[00:53] Tom Barlow: do you capture the actual prompt or model payload? that's the big question for us re PII.
[01:03] Ethan Shaw: short answer: by default we capture request/response metadata but not full unredacted prompt text for enterprise plans unless you opt in. we do provide options: (1) full payload capture for approved legal/forensic cases, (2) redacted fields where we hash or truncate tokens, or (3) no payload capture and only metadata.
[01:25] Priya Singh: can we get an example of the JSONL export so our DLP team can validate patterns?
[01:32] Maya Patel: absolutely, I'll include JSONL and a CSV sample. also a syslog example for SIEM ingestion.
[01:40] Lena Morales: on encryption, are audit logs encrypted with our customer key?
[01:44] Ethan Shaw: yes; for Private and Dedicated we support customer-managed keys (CMKs) via KMS. we integrate with major cloud KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault) and can bring-your-own-key. we also offer HSM-backed keys for higher assurance. logs at rest are encrypted; in transit is TLS 1.2+ with mutual TLS options for streaming.
[02:05] Tom Barlow: great. how about real-time streaming vs batch exports? which do customers use more?
[02:12] Ethan Shaw: common patterns: SIEMs prefer near-real-time syslog/Kinesis streams for alerts, security teams use a streaming path. For long term archival, many customers use daily S3 exports (JSONL or Parquet) and then lifecycle to Glacier/Cold. We support both simultaneously.
[02:30] Lena Morales: retention — we need a legal hold for certain user accounts potentially beyond our baseline three years. can you do selective retention/hold?
[02:38] Maya Patel: yes, we support selective holds. you can tag events or specific user IDs and place them on hold; automated garbage collection will skip held items. there's an API to lift/inspect holds.
[02:50] Priya Singh: is there an audit trail for admin actions in Redwood console itself? we need to show who changed RBAC roles.
[02:58] Ethan Shaw: console admin actions are first-class events: role changes, SSO mappings, user invites, policy changes — we log actor, previous state, new state, and a diff when possible. those are included in the same export streams. occasionally the auto-transcriber here calls it "RBAC SSO" as three words, which is fine, haha.
[03:20] Tom Barlow: about identities, we use Okta groups. can you map Okta group sync to Redwood roles so audit logs show group names not just user ids?
[03:30] Ethan Shaw: yes; our SSO connector can sync groups and we store both group id and display name in the event. we also include the SAML assertion id on demand to link to identity provider logs.
[03:45] Lena Morales: any caveats re attribution across service accounts vs human users? we need to differentiate automation.
[03:52] Ethan Shaw: we tag actor_type: human | service. Service account events include the key fingerprint and optional deploy tag. We recommend rotating service keys and we capture key id which you can correlate to CI/CD.
[04:06] Priya Singh: how long do you keep keys/rotations info? is there an audit of key rotation events?
[04:12] Ethan Shaw: key rotations are logged as events (who rotated, key id, previous key fingerprint), retained according to your retention settings. For CMK operations that happen in customer KMS, we log the Redwood-side reference but the key material is never in Redwood logs.
[04:28] Maya Patel: quick note on model variants: when we fallback to cheaper quantized variants we log the variant used per request so you can see quality regressions over time.
[04:38] Tom Barlow: nice. volume question: roughly how many events per 1M tokens or per 10k requests? we need sizing for S3 and SIEM ingest costs.
[04:48] Ethan Shaw: event size depends on capture mode. metadata-only events typically ~1-2KB; full payload capture can be 5-50KB depending on sequence length. For planning assume 1.5KB per metadata event; we'll include an example spreadsheet in the follow up.
[05:05] Lena Morales: can exports include a manifest and checksums for forensic integrity?
[05:11] Ethan Shaw: yes — daily manifests with SHA256 checksums, s3 ETags, and optional signed attestations. We can feed those to your integrity monitoring.
[05:22] Priya Singh: about evidence packages — do you provide a packaged forensic bundle for legal requests?
[05:28] Maya Patel: we can produce an evidence bundle containing the event JSONL, manifest, and relevant policy context. We also include a derivation of redact rules applied. This is typically scoped and gated by legal review.
[05:44] Tom Barlow: what about data residency? we need logs to remain in EU for our EU customers.
[05:50] Ethan Shaw: we have region-scoped export endpoints. For Hosted customers we offer EU-region retention and storage. For Dedicated/Private you can pin to a VPC region. Exports to S3 or GCS can be targeted to the region you specify. We'll surface residency in the export config.
[06:05] Lena Morales: are there built-in retention policies templates? we have a security baseline and a legal baseline that differ per record type.
[06:12] Maya Patel: yes; we provide retention policy templates (security_short, legal_long, compliance_gdpr) you can apply to event classes. Policies can be time-based or size-based and support conditional retention by actor or tag.
[06:26] Priya Singh: GDPR: can you support the right to be forgotten? if a user requests deletion, are audit trails removed that would break forensic chain?
[06:35] Ethan Shaw: good question. we support pseudonymization and redaction workflows: you can scrub PII from events but maintain an event skeleton (timestamp/action) for auditability. For legal erasure requests we can redact identifying fields while keeping integrity metadata. We log the erasure action itself as an event.
[06:56] Tom Barlow: are redactions reversible? we need to ensure compliance not to be able to re-identify unintentionally.
[07:02] Ethan Shaw: redaction is irreversible from Redwood storage for customer-requested scrubs — we keep a record that a scrub occurred and link to the erasure request id.
[07:12] Lena Morales: ok that helps. backups: do you replicate exports to an immutable store? we like write-once storage for evidence.
[07:19] Maya Patel: we support S3 Object Lock (WORM) via the customer's destination bucket and can propose a workflow to write exports to a locked prefix for retention.
[07:28] Priya Singh: on access controls, who at Redwood can access raw exported logs?
[07:33] Ethan Shaw: internal access is tightly controlled: only ops staff with specific approved JIT requests, MFA, and just-in-time approval can access. All access is logged and we keep an internal audit trail. For enterprise customers we can set a stricter access policy.
[07:47] Tom Barlow: do you provide a schema for the events? our SIEM needs mapping rules.
[07:53] Ethan Shaw: yes, we'll share the event schema, sample events, and a mapping guide for Splunk, Elastic, and Sumo. It'll include field names, types, and typical values.
[08:05] Lena Morales: what about alerting? can you emit a high-priority stream for suspicious admin actions?
[08:12] Ethan Shaw: you can define rules in Redwood Optimize to flag anomalies (e.g., mass role changes, atypical IPs). Those alerts can be forwarded to your SIEM as high-sev events or to pager duty.
[08:24] Priya Singh: how long do you keep the audit index for fast search vs cold storage?
[08:30] Ethan Shaw: default is 90 days for hot search; after that data moves to warm/slow index with slower query times. You can configure hot window to be shorter or longer at cost. Exports to S3 remain for your archival windows.
[08:45] Tom Barlow: integration specifics: for real-time streaming do you support syslog over TLS, Kinesis, and PubSub?
[08:52] Ethan Shaw: yes — syslog over TLS, Kinesis, GCP PubSub, and Kafka (for Dedicated/Private). We'll provide connection docs and cert rotation guidance.
[09:05] Maya Patel: let's talk about retention enforcement: if a retention policy expires, what's the deletion model?
[09:11] Ethan Shaw: deletion is a two-step process: first the event is marked expired then a GC job removes payloads and then metadata after a configurable lag so you have a short recovery window. For held events the GC will skip them. We also support purge-only-if-confirmed for legal workflows.
[09:28] Priya Singh: do you support immutable snapshots for e-discovery?
[09:33] Ethan Shaw: yes — we can create immutable snapshots and export them as an evidence package. Snapshots include manifest and signed attestations.
[09:41] Tom Barlow: SLA for export delivery? we need guarantees for streaming and batch latencies.
[09:47] Ethan Shaw: for Dedicated we can guarantee 99.9% delivery latency under the SLA windows. For Hosted we provide best-effort with 95th percentile targets; we'll include specific numbers in the follow-up.
[09:59] Lena Morales: do you offer a playbook for incident response and audit pull requests?
[10:04] Maya Patel: yes; we'll share a runbook that includes steps to request evidence, contact points, expected timelines, and the format of exported bundles.
[10:12] Priya Singh: question about retention costs: do you have tooling to forecast storage costs for different retention policies?
[10:18] Ethan Shaw: Redwood Console has a cost estimator for exports; you can plug projected event rates and retention windows to see S3 and ingest costs. We'll also include a sample cost spreadsheet.
[10:30] Tom Barlow: about KMS key rotation: if we rotate CMKs frequently will that break past evidence?
[10:36] Ethan Shaw: no — exported logs are encrypted under envelope encryption. The envelope keys are re-encrypted with the new CMK; as long as you retain the old key material in your KMS key version history, we can decrypt archives. We'll document the key rotation best practices.
[10:55] Priya Singh: are there any limitations with on-prem/private deployments?
[11:01] Ethan Shaw: private deployments give you total control over residency and keys; the only extra responsibility is running the export target (you typically manage the destination bucket/collector). We provide the connectors and code to run collectors.
[11:12] Lena Morales: for the pilot, we want a small sample: 24 hours of metadata-only events and one day of full-payload for a few user flows. can Redwood do that?
[11:21] Ethan Shaw: yes — we can spin up a pilot stream and set capture mode per route. we'll keep it scoped.
[11:28] Maya Patel: ok, quick recap and deliverables — I'll list them:
[11:32] Maya Patel: 1) Send JSONL / CSV / syslog export samples and event schema (Maya) by 2025-10-24.
[11:38] Maya Patel: 2) Pilot ingest for 24-48 hours (Ethan) and perf sheet by 2025-10-30.
[11:44] Maya Patel: 3) Customer to confirm exact retention window and residency for regulated accounts (Lena/Priya) by 2025-10-27.
[11:50] Maya Patel: 4) Share SOC2/ISO artifacts and evidence playbook (Maya) — we'll aim to attach SOC2 within the follow-up email.
[12:00] Tom Barlow: for the export samples, please include both minimal and full payload capture so we can size costs.
[12:05] Ethan Shaw: will do; sample spreadsheet with event sizes and projected monthly cost per retention window included.
[12:12] Priya Singh: thanks — also please include an example of the legal-hold API call and a sample evidence package.
[12:18] Maya Patel: noted.
[12:25] Lena Morales: last question: do you produce a cryptographic attestation for tamper-proof evidence?
[12:30] Ethan Shaw: we can sign manifests and include timestamped attestations; for higher assurance we can integrate with third-party timestamping authorities.
[12:40] Maya Patel: awesome. looks like we're aligned on next steps. I'll follow up with the artifacts and scheduling the pilot.

Meeting close / quick notes: transcription imperfect in spots; action owners captured above. Follow-up to include exports, schema, pilot and SOC2 docs.

End of transcript.
